Unlike Sommer et al.'s method, which computes gradients from a second copy of the volume in main memory (slower for translucent projections), this method uses hardware interpolation for throughput [S2].

The claim states that Sommer et al.'s method computes gradients from a second copy of the volume in main memory (which is slower for translucent projections) and that the current method uses hardware interpolation for throughput. Source [S2] explicitly confirms both points: it states that Sommer et al. 'employ a full lighting equation by computing a smooth gradient from a second copy of the volume stored in main memory' and notes that for translucent projections, this takes significantly longer (33.2 seconds vs 2.71 seconds for isosurface). It also states that the proposed method pre-computes gradients and uses '3D texture mapping hardware' to interpolate them, thereby achieving hardware acceleration/throughput.

Runtime complexity is dominated by texture sampling and shading, which is efficient due to hardware interpolation [S2].

The evidence explicitly states that the method pre-computes gradients and stores them in texture memory alongside density data. It further confirms that '3D texture mapping hardware' is used to 'interpolate gradient values and raw density' during the sampling process.
